title: Battery mowers, trimmers and blowers: safe teardown
summary: Battery mowers, trimmers and blowers give a 40–80 V lithium-ion pack, a brushless motor with its controller, switches and a mains charger. Check every pack for swelling, heat and a sweet smell before you charge or open anything: at these voltages a pack can shock you, and a short makes an arc that burns and starts fires.

steps.text: Before you touch the tool, look, feel and smell. Open the battery cover and look at each pack where it sits. Feel the cover and the pack with the back of your hand. If anything is hot while idle, bulging, cracked, hissing, smoking or smells sweet, back off and follow safety_swollen_lithium.
steps.warn: A hot or hissing pack can burst into flame. Don't pull it out by hand: carry it out on a shovel or metal tray to bare ground, sand or concrete, well away from anything that burns.

steps.text: Release the bail bar or trigger and take out the safety key or electric-start button if there is one. Then press the release and slide every battery pack out of the tool. Check every battery bay. The makers say to do this before any servicing, cleaning or clearing (Toro 21466 manual, EGO LM2000E manual).
steps.warn: Even with the power off, a mower blade can still move, and it is sharp (Toro 21466 manual, EGO LM2000E manual). Keep hands away from the deck, a trimmer head, hedge-trimmer blades or a saw chain until every pack is out.

steps.text: Set up outdoors on concrete or stone, away from anything that burns, with a bucket of dry sand and a metal tin to hand. Look over each pack closely: swelling, cracks, dents, melted plastic, rust, water inside, a changed colour or shape. Read the label too. Any damaged or recalled pack: don't charge it or use it. Tape its terminals and store it as in safety_swollen_lithium.
steps.warn: Greenworks says to stop using a pack at once if it smells unusual, feels hot, changes colour or changes shape, and never to charge a cracked one.

steps.text: Measure each sound-looking pack with the meter on DC volts, red probe on the + terminal and black on the −. Rest the probe tips on the contacts gently; don't force them in, because the terminals can bend (Toro 60V service, which is written for models 20363 and 20366). Write the reading on the pack, then cover both terminals with strong tape.
steps.warn: These packs run at 40–80 V DC. That can give a real shock, and a short across the terminals makes an arc that burns skin and starts fires. Never let a probe tip, tool or ring bridge two terminals.

steps.text: If a pack reads healthy and you want to keep it working, test it on its own charger. Put the pack on stone or a metal tray in a well-ventilated place, between 5 and 40 °C (41–104 °F) (Toro 21466 manual), and stay with it. Unplug at once if the pack gets warm. Use only the charger made for that pack.
steps.warn: Never charge a pack that failed the checks in step 3, and never charge below freezing: it can damage the cells for good (OSHA SHIB 06-20-2019).

steps.text: Unplug the charger from the wall and keep it whole with its cord. It is a mains power supply. Don't open it: if you ever must, treat it like any mains charger (teardown_phone_charger, safety_discharge_capacitor).

Mowers: take the blade off now. Wear thick gloves. Lay the mower on its side on cardboard, wedge a block of wood between the blade and the deck, and undo the blade bolt. Keep the washer, blade adapter and any blade-brake parts in the order they came off. The Toro 21466 blade bolt is tightened to 68 N·m (50 ft-lb), so expect it to be tight (Toro 21466 manual).
steps.warn: The blade is sharp. Brace yourself so your hand can't slide onto the edge when the bolt breaks free. A mower is heavy (26.2 kg for the EGO LM2000E, 30.5 kg for the Greenworks MO40L03, both without the pack): get a helper to tip it.

steps.text: Open the motor housing. On the Toro 20363 and 20366 (the models the Toro service manual covers; it does not cover the 21466), 8 flange screws hold the upper shroud (6 round the battery cavity, 2 at the bottom rear), then 4 T20 Torx screws hold the motor fan shroud (Toro 60V service). Other Toro models and other makes differ: look under labels and in the battery bay for hidden screws. Photograph the wiring before you unplug anything.

Prove the controller dead before you touch it. Wait at least 5 minutes after the last pack came out. Check your meter on a charged pack first. Then measure DC volts across the battery-receiver contacts in the tool and across the controller's power input once you can reach it. You want under 1 V. If it's higher, discharge the controller's capacitors with a resistor tool (safety_discharge_capacitor) and measure again. Then check the meter on the pack once more.
steps.warn: If the meter didn't read the pack before and after, its zero proved nothing. Don't trust a zero from an untested meter.

steps.text: Unplug the battery receiver from the controller: on the Toro 20363 and 20366, positive first, then negative (Toro 60V service; it does not cover the 21466). Now the controller's own power input pins are bare, so measure across them: you want under 1 V. Then clip a wire across them and leave it there while you work. Put tape over the battery bay so nobody slides a pack in.
steps.warn: Never put a shorting wire across the battery receiver itself: a pack slid in later would be dead-shorted.

steps.text: Unplug the rest of the controller's harness (the start and bail switch plugs, the motor's harness plug and the motor power connection) and undo its screws. Lift it out with its loom and plugs; label each plug with tape (Toro 60V service lists these plugs for the 20363 and 20366).

Undo the motor's mounting screws, holding the motor or having a helper hold it as the last one comes out (the Toro service manual says to support the motor with a lifting device at that point on the 20363: Toro 60V service). Then lift it out with its fan. Count the thick wires from the motor: three means a brushless motor that needs its controller; two means a brushed DC motor (skill_identify_motors).

Take the small parts: the bail or trigger switch, start switch, battery receiver, wiring harness and LED lights. Self-propelled mowers: unbolt the drive transmission, its belt and the rear wheels with their bearings (Toro 21466 parts). Blowers: take the fan off the motor; the Ryobi RY404010 lists a fan and an M6 flange lock nut (Ryobi RY404010 sheet). The Toro 21466 parts list shows two magnets with the hood and upper shroud (Toro 21466 parts).

Open a pack only if it is dead for good and you want its cells. The makers say never to open one (Toro 21466 manual, EGO LM2000E manual). Work outdoors on concrete with sand to hand. Take off rings and watches, and wear gloves and eye protection (Toro 21466 manual says gloves and eye protection when servicing). Take out every screw first. If the case is glued, warm the seam with a hair dryer on low, keeping it under 54 °C (130 °F), and work along it with plastic tools only. If it won't open without force, leave it whole. Any puffed, wet or hot cell inside: stop and follow safety_swollen_lithium.
steps.warn: Never push a blade or screwdriver into a seam or use a heat gun: a damaged cell can start a fire in seconds.

steps.text: Inside the pack, cut the main leads one at a time and tape each cut end before you cut the next. The cells are still joined in one long series string at the full pack voltage. Before you peel any strip, split the string: cut the strips between cell groups one at a time with insulated-handle cutters, keeping the cutter jaws off the cell tops and taping each cut end, until no section has more than about 8 cells in series (under about 34 V at 4.2 V a cell). Then separate the cells or blocks as in teardown_laptop_battery and measure each one (test_lithium_cell).
steps.warn: Never cut two wires in one bite. One slip across a 40–80 V pack makes an arc that burns skin and starts fires.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The tool and its packs, working.** A mower, trimmer or blower with good packs and its charger is worth more whole than in parts. Packs and chargers belong to one brand's system: on the Toro 20363 and 20366 the pack sleeps until the mower or charger wakes it through a communication line, and the charger has its own communication terminal (Toro 60V service, which covers those models, not the 21466). Toro warns that a charger for one type of pack can start a fire on another (Toro 21466 manual).
- **Battery packs.** Toro's 88660 is rated 6.0 Ah and 324 Wh, 60 V maximum and 54 V nominal (Toro 21466 manual). On the 20363 and 20366, a healthy Toro pack reads 43–62 V; the mower stops at 43 V, the charger stops at 62 V, and a pack under 40 V is over-discharged and will most likely not recover (Toro 60V service). The 21466's pack may differ. Greenworks' BAF704 is 36 V nominal (sold as 40 V MAX), 4.0 Ah, 144 Wh, with a USB-A port (Greenworks BAF manual). The 20363 and 20366 pack holds an internal fuse that can't be replaced, and Toro's manual for those models checks for a blown one by testing across the + and − terminals (Toro 60V service). A good pack may run a 12 V system through a DC-DC converter rated well above the pack's full-charge voltage, with a fuse at the pack. A brand's pack may stay asleep until its own tool or charger wakes it (Toro 60V service, for the 20363 and 20366), so try one first. A pack that won't work whole can give cells for smaller packs (build_18650_pack).
- **Charger.** Toro's 88602 takes 120 V AC and gives 60 V MAX DC at 2.0 A (Toro 21466 manual). On the 20363 and 20366 the charger has an internal fuse that isn't serviceable and a fan that cools a hot pack before charging (Toro 60V service; the 21466 may differ). Keep it with the packs it fits.
- **Motor.** The Toro 20363 and 20366 use a 2 kW brushless DC motor with cooling fans on top (Toro 60V service); the 21466 parts list names a Motor-2Kw (Toro 21466 parts), so count its wires to check that it is brushless. Greenworks' MO40L03 is brushless and runs 2,800 rpm at no load on 40 V (Greenworks MO40L03 manual). With its own controller and pack it drives a pump, fan or grinder at that voltage. Spun by hand, wind or water, a brushless motor makes three-phase AC that a rectifier turns into DC (test_motor).
- **Controller.** On the Toro 20363 and 20366 the service manual calls it the motor driver, and the 21466 parts list calls it the Controller-Motor; Greenworks calls it a power control board; Ryobi pairs the motor controller with the blower's inlet bell (Toro 60V service, Toro 21466 parts, Greenworks MO40L03 manual, Ryobi RY404010 sheet). Reuse it only with its own motor and pack voltage, and keep its switch wiring: the 20363 and 20366 driver is wired to the start and bail switches (Toro 60V service).
- **Switches, battery receiver, harness and lights.** Toro lists a bail switch, a starter switch, a battery receiver and a wire harness (Toro 21466 parts). Ryobi's blower has a signal switch and a push switch (Ryobi RY404010 sheet).
- **Drive parts.** The Toro 21466 has a rear-wheel transmission, a V-belt and two ball bearings (Toro 21466 parts). On the EGO LM2130SP the self-propel drive is a separate unit with its own motor, and the rear wheels hold gears (iFixit EGO LM2130SP).

## Shock, fire and heat

- OSHA treats any voltage of 50 V or more as hazardous, AC or DC, and reports serious injuries from contact with live DC parts at 50–100 V (OSHA 50 V letter). Greenworks warns of electric shock from its 40 V MAX packs (Greenworks BAF manual).
- Shorting the terminals can cause burns or a fire. Under abuse a pack can eject liquid that irritates or burns: flush skin with water (Toro 21466 manual, EGO LM2000E manual).
- Lithium cells are damaged by heat above about 54 °C (130 °F) and by charging below freezing (OSHA SHIB 06-20-2019). Toro says never to heat its pack above 68 °C (154 °F) and to charge and store it at 5–40 °C (Toro 21466 manual).
- For storage, Toro says to leave the pack part charged (2 or 3 of its 4 lights), not full or empty, and not outside or in a vehicle (Toro 21466 manual).
- Recalls: SKIL 40V 5.0Ah packs, model BY8708-00 made before 1 May 2021, can overheat; the maker had 100 reports of overheating, melting, smoke or fire (CPSC SKIL 40V recall). Ten RYOBI 40 V 21-inch mower models have a push-on connector in the powerhead that can overheat (97 reports, 5 fires) (CPSC Ryobi 40V mower recall). Treat a recalled unit as damaged.

## Variations

- **Toro 21466:** 60 V MAX walk mower, pack 88660, charger 88602, Motor-2Kw with a separate controller, rear-wheel drive (Toro 21466 manual, Toro 21466 parts). The Toro service manual covers models 20363 and 20366, not the 21466, so its figures and steps may differ on this one (Toro 60V service).
- **EGO LM2000E:** 56 V mower, 51 cm deck, 26.2 kg without the pack, a blade brake and a removable safety key. Count the thick wires from its motor to tell brushed from brushless (skill_identify_motors).
- **Greenworks MO40L03:** 40 V brushless mower, motor R0201026-00, power control board R0201043-00, pack BAF704, charger CAF806 (Greenworks MO40L03 manual).
- **Ryobi RY404010:** 40 V brushless blower: motor, motor controller with inlet bell, fan, two switches and a grounding strap (Ryobi RY404010 sheet).
- Screw types, how the shrouds come apart and where the controller sits differ by maker. Check yours as you go.

## What to leave

- Swollen, cracked, hot, wet or recalled packs: store them as in safety_swollen_lithium.
- A pack you can't open without forcing a blade into a seam.
- The inside of the charger.
- The plastic deck and shrouds, unless you need them.

## Testing what you got out

- **Pack:** the voltage check in step 4, then a watched charge on its own charger.
- **Motor:** spin the shaft by hand with the meter on AC volts between each pair of the three thick wires. Three similar readings that rise with speed mean the windings are sound.
- **Controller:** Toro's check for the 20363 and 20366 is: pack good, voltage reaching the driver, motor good; if all three pass and it still won't run, the driver is at fault (Toro 60V service).
